outputs.L1:
The present invention discloses a mechanically strengthened piezoelectric sensor for Structural Health Monitoring applications. The sensor comprises a two-sided piezo ceramic component, a sensor encapsulation, and at least two wires. The sensor encapsulation includes an indented side defining a recessed area, within which a supporting structure is provided. The two-sided piezo ceramic component is mounted within the recessed area of the encapsulation and supported by the supporting structure, with the outward-facing side positioned slightly below the upper edge of the recessed area. The supporting structure of the encapsulation provides mechanical reinforcement to the piezo ceramic component. The wires are attached to the electrodes of the piezo ceramic component and extend outward from the encapsulation.

Alternatively, the mechanically strengthened piezoelectric sensor may further include a Printed Circuit Board (PCB). In this configuration, the piezo ceramic component is mounted on the PCB, and the PCB is then mounted within the recessed area of the encapsulation and supported by the supporting structure, with the outward-facing side positioned slightly below the upper edge of the encapsulation.

The invention describes a piezoelectric sensor with enhanced mechanical robustness for use in Structural Health Monitoring. The device comprises a piezoceramic element having two active sides, an encapsulating body, and no fewer than two electrical leads. One side of the encapsulation is provided with an indentation that defines a cavity. Within this cavity is a support feature. The two-sided piezoceramic element is placed inside the cavity of the encapsulation and rests on the support feature, with its outward-facing surface positioned slightly below the top rim of the cavity. The support feature in the encapsulation reinforces the piezoceramic element mechanically. The wires are connected to the electrodes of the piezoceramic element and pass outward from the encapsulation.

In another configuration, the mechanically reinforced piezoelectric sensor may also contain a Printed Circuit Board (PCB). In this version, the piezoceramic element is first secured to the PCB. The PCB is then installed in the cavity of the encapsulation and supported by the support feature, with the outward-facing side positioned slightly below the upper edge of the encapsulation.
outputs.L3:
The invention relates to a mechanically strengthened piezoelectric sensor intended for use in Structural Health Monitoring (SHM) applications. Such sensors are designed to be attached to or integrated into structures in order to detect mechanical changes, vibrations, strain, damage, or other structural conditions over time. The proposed design improves the mechanical robustness of the sensor while maintaining its ability to generate and receive piezoelectric signals.

The sensor comprises a piezo ceramic component having two opposite sides, each provided with an electrode. At least two electrical wires are connected to these electrodes, allowing the piezo ceramic component to be electrically coupled to external measuring, control, or data acquisition equipment. The piezo ceramic component is arranged within a sensor encapsulation that protects the component from environmental influences and mechanical damage.

The sensor encapsulation includes an indented side that forms a recessed area. This recessed area is shaped to receive the piezo ceramic component and includes a supporting structure. The supporting structure provides mechanical reinforcement for the piezo ceramic component and helps distribute forces acting on the sensor during use. By supporting the piezo ceramic component in this way, the risk of cracking, chipping, or other mechanical failure of the ceramic material is reduced.

The piezo ceramic component is mounted within the recessed area of the encapsulation such that its outward-facing side is positioned slightly below the upper edge of the encapsulation. This arrangement provides additional protection because the piezo ceramic component does not protrude beyond the surrounding encapsulation. As a result, the encapsulation can absorb or shield the component from direct mechanical contact, impacts, or abrasion.

In one embodiment, the piezo ceramic component is placed directly into the recessed area and supported by the supporting structure of the encapsulation. In an alternative embodiment, the piezo ceramic component is first mounted on a printed circuit board (PCB). The PCB carrying the piezo ceramic component is then arranged within the recessed area of the sensor encapsulation. This configuration can simplify electrical connection, improve handling during assembly, and provide additional mechanical support to the piezo ceramic component.

Overall, the invention provides a robust piezoelectric sensor construction suitable for demanding SHM environments. By positioning the piezo ceramic component within a recessed encapsulation and reinforcing it with a supporting structure, the sensor achieves improved durability while preserving the functional properties required for structural monitoring.
outputs.L4:
The invention relates to a piezoelectric sensor assembly, in particular for use in Structural Health Monitoring applications, where sensors are required to remain operational over long periods of time under mechanical load, vibration, temperature variation, humidity, and other environmental influences. In many monitoring systems, piezoelectric ceramic elements are bonded to or embedded in a structure in order to detect acoustic emissions, strain-induced signals, vibrations, impacts, cracks, delamination, or other structural changes. However, such ceramic components are often brittle and sensitive to handling damage, edge chipping, bending loads, and external mechanical impacts. There is therefore a need for a robust sensor construction that protects the piezoelectric element while maintaining reliable electromechanical coupling and electrical connectivity.

The invention addresses this need by providing a sensor module comprising a piezoelectric ceramic component having two electrically active sides. The piezoelectric ceramic component may be arranged directly within the module or may optionally be mounted on a printed circuit board, for example to facilitate electrical contacting, signal routing, impedance matching, or integration with additional electronic components. The piezoelectric ceramic component is positioned within an encapsulation body that includes a recessed region or cavity. This recessed configuration allows the active ceramic component to be received inside the encapsulation rather than protruding from it, thereby reducing the likelihood that the ceramic will be damaged during manufacture, installation, handling, or use.

A supporting structure is provided within the encapsulation to mechanically support and strengthen the piezoelectric ceramic component. The supporting structure may be formed as a frame, rib, shoulder, support platform, spacer, or similar reinforcing element. It is arranged so that it stabilizes the piezoelectric component and, where present, the printed circuit board, while also protecting the edges and surfaces of the ceramic element from direct mechanical contact. By distributing mechanical stresses away from the ceramic component, the supporting structure reduces the risk of cracking or fracture. At the same time, the construction preserves the functional ability of the piezoelectric component to receive and/or generate mechanical waves or electrical signals relevant to structural monitoring.

The piezoelectric ceramic component is preferably positioned slightly below the outer edge or rim of the encapsulation. In other words, the encapsulation forms a protective boundary that extends marginally beyond the exposed level of the ceramic component. This recessed placement provides a protective buffer against abrasion, impact, and compressive forces applied from outside the module. Because the ceramic component does not project beyond the encapsulation edge, accidental contact with tools, adjacent structures, or installation fixtures is less likely to damage the sensor. The recessed arrangement also allows the sensor module to be handled and mounted more safely and consistently.

Electrical connections are provided from the two sides of the piezoelectric ceramic component to external wires. These wire connections allow the sensor to be connected to monitoring electronics, data acquisition units, signal conditioning circuits, or control systems. The external wires may be routed through or out of the encapsulation in a protected manner, and may be connected to the piezoelectric element directly or through conductive traces on the optional printed circuit board. The two-sided electrical configuration enables the piezoelectric ceramic component to function as an active sensing element, an actuator, or a combined actuator-sensor element, depending on the monitoring system in which it is used.

The encapsulation may be made from a polymer, resin, composite, elastomer, or other protective material suitable for the intended operating environment. It may protect the piezoelectric ceramic component against moisture, dust, chemicals, and mechanical wear, while also providing a defined geometry for installation. The encapsulation can be configured for bonding to a structure, embedding in a composite material, attachment to a surface, or integration into a larger monitoring assembly. The recessed cavity and supporting structure cooperate to provide both mechanical protection and reliable positioning of the piezoelectric component.

In use, the sensor module may be attached to a structure whose integrity is to be monitored, such as an aircraft component, wind turbine blade, bridge element, pipeline, pressure vessel, vehicle component, machine part, or composite panel. Mechanical waves, vibrations, acoustic emissions, or strain-related disturbances in the structure are transmitted to the piezoelectric component, which converts them into electrical signals. These signals can then be analyzed to identify damage, degradation, impact events, or changes in structural condition. Because the piezoelectric ceramic component is mechanically supported and recessed within the encapsulation, the sensor is more resistant to damage and is therefore better suited for long-term monitoring applications.

The invention thus provides a durable and reliable piezoelectric sensor construction for Structural Health Monitoring. By combining a two-sided piezoelectric ceramic component, optional printed circuit board mounting, protected external wire connections, a recessed encapsulation, and an internal supporting structure, the sensor module achieves improved robustness without sacrificing sensing functionality. The supporting structure strengthens and protects the brittle ceramic component, while the recessed placement below the encapsulation edge reduces exposure to external mechanical damage. As a result, the sensor can provide improved reliability, easier handling, and longer service life in demanding monitoring environments.
outputs.L5:
**The Importance of Structural Health**

Structural health refers to the condition, strength, and safety of buildings, bridges, tunnels, and other engineered structures. Maintaining structural health is essential because these structures support daily life, transportation, business, and public safety. Over time, materials can weaken due to weather, heavy use, vibration, corrosion, or natural disasters such as earthquakes and floods.

Engineers monitor structural health through inspections, sensors, and advanced technology. These methods help detect cracks, movement, stress, or damage before they become serious problems. By identifying risks early, repairs can be made more efficiently, reducing costs and preventing accidents.

The structural health of any building or infrastructure system should never be ignored. Regular maintenance, proper design, and continuous monitoring help extend the life of structures and protect the people who use them. In modern engineering, structural health is a key part of creating safe, reliable, and sustainable communities.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a concise patent-style description for a piezoelectric sensor assembly where a piezo ceramic component is recessed below the edge of an encapsulation and mechanically strengthened by internal supports.
counterfactuals.output:
A piezoelectric sensor assembly includes an encapsulation body having a peripheral edge and defining a recess within which a piezoelectric ceramic component is disposed. The piezoelectric ceramic component is positioned below the peripheral edge of the encapsulation body such that the edge provides mechanical shielding against direct impact or abrasion. Electrical contacts are coupled to opposing electrode surfaces of the piezoelectric ceramic component and extend through or along the encapsulation body for connection to external circuitry.

The encapsulation body includes one or more internal support structures arranged adjacent to, beneath, or around the piezoelectric ceramic component. The internal support structures mechanically reinforce the piezoelectric ceramic component and distribute forces applied to the sensor assembly through the encapsulation body, thereby reducing localized stress on the piezoelectric ceramic component. The internal support structures may comprise ribs, pillars, webs, frames, or filled support regions integrally formed with or bonded to the encapsulation body.

In operation, mechanical loading applied to the sensor assembly is transmitted to the piezoelectric ceramic component in a controlled manner while the recessed arrangement and internal supports protect the component from fracture, chipping, and excessive bending. The assembly thereby provides improved durability while maintaining sensitivity to pressure, vibration, strain, or impact forces.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an invention disclosure paragraph describing a strengthened piezoelectric sensor for structural health monitoring, including both direct mounting of the piezo ceramic and an alternative PCB-mounted embodiment.
counterfactuals.output: A strengthened piezoelectric sensor for structural health monitoring is disclosed, comprising a piezoelectric ceramic sensing element configured to be mechanically coupled to a monitored structure to detect strain, vibration, acoustic emission, or guided-wave response. In one embodiment, the piezoelectric ceramic is directly mounted to the surface of the structure using a structural adhesive or bonding layer that provides high-fidelity strain transfer, with electrical leads coupled to opposing electrodes of the ceramic and a protective reinforcement layer, encapsulant, or ruggedized cover disposed over and/or around the ceramic to improve impact resistance, moisture resistance, fatigue life, and durability under field conditions. The reinforcement may include a composite patch, polymer overmold, metal or fiber-reinforced cover, or strain-distributing layer selected to protect the brittle ceramic while maintaining sufficient electromechanical coupling to the structure. In an alternative embodiment, the piezoelectric ceramic is mounted on a printed circuit board (PCB) that provides electrical routing, connectorization, impedance matching, shielding, signal conditioning components, or identification circuitry, and the PCB assembly is bonded or mechanically attached to the monitored structure such that structural strain or wave energy is transmitted through the PCB and/or an intermediate coupling layer to the piezoelectric element. The PCB-mounted embodiment may include local stiffening, compliant coupling regions, vias, guard traces, encapsulation, and protective packaging to balance sensor robustness with sensitivity. Both embodiments provide a rugged piezoelectric transducer suitable for long-term structural health monitoring of assets such as bridges, aircraft, vehicles, pipelines, wind turbines, buildings, or industrial equipment.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a technical summary of a mechanically reinforced piezo sensor with a two-sided piezo ceramic, encapsulation recess, support structure, outward-facing side below the upper edge, and wires extending from electrodes.
counterfactuals.output:
A mechanically reinforced piezo sensor comprises a two-sided piezoelectric ceramic element with electrodes provided on opposite faces for signal generation. Electrical wires extend from the respective electrodes to provide external electrical connection.

The piezo ceramic is arranged within an encapsulation or housing recess that mechanically protects the ceramic while allowing it to receive mechanical loading. A support structure surrounds or supports the ceramic in the recess and is configured to reinforce the sensor against impact, bending, compression, or installation loads. The support structure can stabilize the ceramic position, reduce stress concentration at the ceramic edges, and improve durability during handling and operation.

The sensor includes an outward-facing side of the piezo ceramic or sensor assembly that is positioned below an upper edge of the encapsulation or surrounding support. This recessed arrangement helps shield the active ceramic surface from direct mechanical damage while still permitting force, pressure, vibration, or acoustic energy to be transmitted to the piezoelectric element. The upper edge may act as a protective rim, stop, or load-distribution feature.

In operation, mechanical deformation, pressure, or vibration applied to the sensor is transferred through the encapsulation and support structure to the piezo ceramic. The ceramic generates an electrical charge or voltage across the electrodes, and the attached wires conduct the resulting signal to external circuitry. The combination of a two-sided electrode configuration, recessed encapsulation, and reinforcing support structure provides a robust piezoelectric sensor suitable for environments requiring improved mechanical protection and reliable signal output.
